title: A delivery platform's price and subscription design can turn convenience into a consumer-recourse problem
source_unit: FTC Instacart enforcement settlement announcement, case materials, and later public-comment notice on online food-delivery fees
geography: United States consumers using Instacart and the federal online food-delivery market

observations.period: December 2025 through April 2026; FTC Instacart settlement and subsequent online-food-delivery fee inquiry

denominator.unit: named federal consumer-protection case and related rulemaking inquiry

pricing_and_subscription_allegations.value: FTC alleged that Instacart advertised free delivery while charging undisclosed service fees on some orders, automatically enrolled some free-trial users into paid Instacart+ memberships without express informed consent, and made cancellation or refund access difficult

redress.unit: US dollars in announced consumer refunds

firm_change.value: proposed order requires the company to stop the challenged practices and provide refunds to consumers charged for memberships without express informed consent
firm_change.unit: reported enforcement remedy and conduct requirement

marketwide_followup.value: FTC later sought public comment on disclosure, refundability, recipients, and consent for fees in online food and grocery delivery

individual_recovery_and_behavior.unit: missing customer-level refund receipt, amount, time cost, continued use, switching, trust, and grocery-cost outcome

observations.method: Review of FTC case-page materials, settlement announcement, complaint summary, and subsequent public-comment notice; alleged practices, announced redress, conduct requirements, and marketwide inquiry are kept as separate stages.
observations.uncertainty: The FTC materials describe allegations and settlement terms, not a representative estimate of all Instacart users' experiences or a measured effect on grocery prices. The public record used here does not show how many consumers received refunds, the average amount, or whether behavior changed.
observations.subgroup: Consumers using Instacart delivery or Instacart+ trials and memberships, including consumers who sought refunds or encountered service fees; nonusers, merchants, shoppers, and consumers with different order patterns are not linked to the case outcome.
observations.counterinterpretation: Delivery platforms can provide valued convenience and some consumers may have understood or accepted the terms. A settlement can resolve legal exposure and change firm rules without showing that every charge was unwanted or that grocery delivery became cheaper afterward.

related_sources.claim: FTC's later public-comment notice extends the case from one firm to marketwide online food and grocery delivery fee practices.
FTC case page records the settlement amount, proposed conduct requirements, and timeline materials.

boundary: This record measures an enforcement allegation, announced redress, firm conduct requirements, and a later marketwide fee inquiry. It does not establish an all-user harm rate, individual refund receipt, lower grocery costs, continued use, switching, or durable consumer trust.
